summary:
La Libertad region stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not a crime, but the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Hate-crime provisions in Peru's Penal Code carry no LGBT coverage after Congress voted in 2017 to strip those protections, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without them.

La Libertad appears in the Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people between 2012 and 2021 with 84 criminal complaints covering 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. La Libertad ranks second in absolute count with 10 of the 88 deaths, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima's 12, with the region's cases centred on Trujillo. Six fiscal districts account for 58% of the deaths: Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). La Libertad's roughly 3% share of national population against an approximately 11.4% share of these deaths gives a per-capita lethality around 3.8 times the national average, a concentration not explained by population alone.

Regionally, Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR, dated 6 September 2024 and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, states that every travesti, transsexual and transgender person in La Libertad has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability. The ordinance cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code, which treats discrimination as a crime, and recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights.

Elsewhere in Peru, enforcement of the bathroom restriction reaches private and public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym that enforced it, and television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told congresswoman Susel Paredes to 'go use the men's room'. Recorded violence against trans people is rising and under-counted: 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed between 2020 and 2023, and a 2024 report co-authored by trans journalist Gianna Camacho found trans women most affected while stressing that recorded figures are a sub-registry.

Two protective rulings sit against that record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of trans woman and activist Azul Rojas Marín, Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. The Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard against which Peru's bathroom law and the removal of hate-crime coverage stand in clear conflict.
tangentialFactors:
The Public Ministry study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and improving monitoring systems. Whether those recommendations were implemented in La Libertad is not stated in the source.

Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR was presented in the regional council's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024, and entered into force the day after its publication in El Peruano. It recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity and orders the establishment of a working group (mesa de trabajo) to carry it out.

The institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found that the national bathroom provision discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring them from facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. Human Rights Watch states that the child-protection framing in the April 2025 law is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Human Rights Watch's characterisation and the IDEHPUCP findings are national-level assessments; no equivalent regional finding for La Libertad is on record in this inventory.
localsOnly:
Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR is a resident-facing instrument of the Regional Government of La Libertad. It declares positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region, in the terms of the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on gender identity or its expression, and it recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.

The ordinance recommends that local governments in La Libertad issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabalho corrected: mesa de trabajo) to take the measures forward. Whether the recommended municipal ordinances have been issued, or whether the working group has been constituted and has met, is not sourced here.

Article 323 of Peru's Penal Code treats discrimination as a crime and is cited in the ordinance as its legal grounding; the ordinance also invokes constitutional equality guarantees and a 2014 regional-council framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity. The national hate-crime provisions, by contrast, carry no LGBT coverage following the 2017 repeal.

Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance in June 2024, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional after an activist legal challenge. Both measures apply nationally, including to health facilities in La Libertad.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Public Ministry's figures run from 2012 to 2021 and are drawn from criminal complaints; regional violence data for La Libertad after 2021, and any breakdown separating trans victims from LGBT victims generally within the region, are not sourced in this inventory. The concentration is calculated against population share, not against urban density in Trujillo, and the source does not test other explanations.

Whether the April 2025 restroom provision or the bans on inclusive signage have been applied to public facilities in La Libertad is unresolved: the inventory records the national law and enforcement examples from elsewhere in Peru, with no regional enforcement record here.

Implementation of Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR is not verifiable from the sources given. There is no sourced evidence on employment outcomes for trans people in La Libertad since publication, on whether municipal ordinances followed the recommendation, or on the composition and activity of the ordered working group.

Whether the 2017 recommendations on prosecutor training and victim-identification monitoring reached La Libertad's fiscal offices is not stated. No regional figure is available on hate-crime reports against trans people in La Libertad, in part because Peru's hate-crime law no longer covers LGBT victims.
